analysis.one_liner: Bans advertisers from targeting ads using people's personal data or identifiers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit advertisers and the companies that place ads for them from targeting ads at individuals based on personal information — browsing history, contact details, device identifiers, or inferred data. It would still allow ordinary contextual advertising (an ad next to a relevant article) and broad geographic targeting down to the level of a town or congressional district, but not tracking of individual people or devices. It would be enforced by the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals suing in court, and it would void arbitration clauses covering these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users whose browsing, location, and contact information would no longer be assembled and sold to target ads at them. That includes people targeted with ads based on sensitive moments — health crises, financial distress — and anyone who wants a cheaper path to law enforcement of their privacy rights, since the bill creates a private right of action with damages and invalidates pre-dispute arbitration clauses for these disputes.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits advertisers and advertising facilitators from targeting ads using personal information, lists of individuals, contact details, or unique device identifiers, and bars sharing that data for targeting [S2].

Allows contextual advertising (based on what a person is currently viewing or searched) and targeting based on a recognized place such as a state, city, or congressional district — so general audience advertising remains legal [S2].

Creates a private right of action with statutory damages from $100 to $5,000 per violation, attorney's fees, and a rule that a violation is itself a concrete injury; and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims [S2].
Gives the FTC enforcement authority over common carriers and nonprofits (closing jurisdictional gaps), and lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The digital advertising industry — platforms like the large social-media and search companies, ad-tech intermediaries, and data brokers whose core business is collecting personal information to target and sell ads. Advertisers that rely on individually targeted campaigns, especially small online businesses that use targeting to reach niche customers efficiently, would also face higher acquisition costs.

drawbacks.text: Small advertisers — including small businesses, nonprofits, and campaigns — currently use cheap, precise ad targeting to reach narrow audiences; a targeting ban would push them toward costlier, less efficient advertising [S2] (the bill's prohibition applies to all advertisers and facilitators, with only contextual and broad-place exceptions).

Much of the free internet is funded by targeted advertising; broad de-targeting could shift revenue and increase ad loads or paywalls for users, and the bill's one-paragraph enforcement design leaves significant transition questions to FTC rulemaking [S2].
The 'recognized place' exception still allows fairly broad geographic targeting, so ads targeted to, say, an entire congressional district or designated market area would remain legal [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are real and large for individuals, and the bill was drafted to preserve contextual and broad-geographic advertising so general-purpose ads survive. The genuine costs fall on advertisers' efficiency and on the ad-funded internet's economics, and the bill gives the FTC two years of rulemaking runway without a detailed transition plan. Weighing honestly: it is a consumer-protective bill whose main cost is borne by a specific, highly concentrated industry, with some spillover to small advertisers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took the bill up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden, joined by Sen. Cory Booker, introduced the Banning Surveillance Advertising Act of 2023 on September 18, 2023 [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S4].
No further action — hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The online advertising industry. Platforms, ad-tech intermediaries, and data brokers keep the current business model — collecting personal information to target and sell ads — unchanged, because the bill never reached even a committee vote. Ordinary users' data continues to be gathered and monetized as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Digital ad platforms and data brokers

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded no further action beyond referral; it stalled in committee with minimal cosponsor support.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; it was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Booker' and the cosponsor list shows one Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Digital advertising industry (platforms, ad-tech firms, data brokers)
against.role: Industry whose business model the bill would ban
against.what_they_did: Opposed surveillance-advertising bans generally; a ban on targeted advertising would strike at the core revenue model of the large ad platforms.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill and no Republican support is recorded; with no hearings or votes, the partisan shape of a full floor fight was never tested.

industries.industry: Online advertising platforms (search and social media giants)
industries.note: Targeting ads with personal data is the core of their ad business; the bill would force a shift to contextual and broad-location advertising, reducing ad value and revenue. Their interest in keeping behavioral tracking runs against users' privacy interests. [S2]
These firms exist to assemble, sell, and use personal information and device identifiers for targeting — exactly what the bill prohibits, including passing identifiers to third parties. [S2]

industries.industry: Small and niche advertisers (small businesses, nonprofits, campaigns)
industries.note: They lose cheap precise targeting but gain from limits on being outbid by data-rich giants and from reduced data-collection exposure; the bill's contextual and broad-place exceptions leave some targeting available. [S2]
Free content funded by targeted ads would earn less per ad, likely increasing ad loads or paywalls; users also gain the privacy protections the same rule creates. [S2]
